body:
in Architecture, History |   	October 23rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Schol­ars dis­agree on when, exact­ly, Rome fell. But if you watch the new video from City 3D Time­lapse above, you’ll under­stand the lack of debate on the ques­tion of whether it fell. Around the turn of the sixth cen­tu­ry AD, build­ings start van­ish­ing at a rate that soon turns alarm­ing; long before the end of the first mil­len­ni­um, it’s clear that Rome has been plunged into very hard times indeed. In the video’s accel­er­at­ed visu­al his­to­ry, that much-scru­ti­nized 500-year span pass­es in a lit­tle more than five sec­onds. Just one minute lat­er, it has spread not just beyond the old city lim­its, but beyond the very frame of the aer­i­al view, becom­ing the vast urban­ized region we know today.
Leg­end has it that Rome was found­ed in 753 BC, when Romu­lus killed his twin broth­er Remus. As reflect­ed by the video, archae­o­log­i­cal evi­dence sug­gests that the area was set­tled ear­li­er, though the tra­di­tion­al date of Rome’s found­ing rough­ly coin­cides with the emer­gence of what we know as the Roman King­dom.
There fol­low the Roman Repub­lic, the Roman Empire, the medieval era — when the once-for­mi­da­ble Eter­nal City was left prac­ti­cal­ly for dead  — the Renais­sance, the Roman Baroque peri­od, the indus­tri­al era, and final­ly, our time of glob­al­iza­tion. For ref­er­ence, the clas­si­cal archae­ol­o­gist Gio­van­ni Pirane­si went to Rome and drew his influ­en­tial etch­ings of its ruins around the 1:55 mark of this three-minute video.
Not that the Rome cap­tured in Pirane­si’s Vedute bears much resem­blance to the Rome of the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry, for bet­ter or for worse. You can still see the Colos­se­um by moon­light, but the ambi­ence won’t be the same: the over­growth has long since been scraped off, and the car­go shorts are out in force year-round. Regard­less, no city is best appre­ci­at­ed through its land­marks alone, not even the mod­ern Rome so long both cel­e­brat­ed and dis­missed as an open-air muse­um. Watch­ing it rise, fall, and rise again from above with­in the length of a Euro­vi­sion song reminds us that it was­n’t built, or rebuilt, in a day — and that, in the face of often-for­mi­da­ble dif­fi­cul­ties, it even now man­ages to put up some­thing new once in a while.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: 'Street Photography Africa' is a Colorful and Energetic Survey Across the Continent
description: From the markets of Dakar and Lagos to the sidewalks of Abidjan and the Beherawi neighborhood of Addis Abab, a bold new book by Nadine Barth and A
body:
From the markets of Dakar and Lagos to the sidewalks of Abidjan and the Beherawi neighborhood of Addis Abab, a bold new book by Nadine Barth and Azu Nwagbogu travels from country to country to present a vast portrait of life on the continent. Street Photography Africa compiles hundreds of images from 33 photographers who each turn their lens to public spaces, documenting cultural moments with musicians and dancers alongside more everyday fashions and routines. While vast in scope, location, and style, the nearly 300-page survey is connected by the central premise that “the street becomes a stage.”
Street Photography Africa is out this month from Thames & Hudson. Find your copy on Bookshop.

title: Wangari Mathenge's Vibrant Paintings Tap into Kenya's Paradigm Shift in the 1960s
description: In 1963, following nearly 70 years of British colonial rule, Kenya declared independence. The nation was not alone on the African continent; in th
body:
In 1963, following nearly 70 years of British colonial rule, Kenya declared independence. The nation was not alone on the African continent; in the 1960s, Gambia, Guyana, Malawi, Nigeria, and others freed themselves from Britain’s control in a watershed period of democratic redevelopment and socio-cultural shifts. Wangari Mathenge, who was born in Nairobi, looks to the not-so-distant past in an ongoing series of vivid oil paintings.
Many of the works shown here are part of the artist’s current solo exhibition, Re-membering at Lévy Gorvy Dayan. Inspired in part by scholar Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s 2009 book Something Torn and New: An African Renaissance, Mathenge examines her own cultural identity through the lens of Kenya in the first half of the 20th century. Something Torn and New focuses on the long-lasting impacts of colonialism and slavery in Africa.
“Re-membering XII (The Wednesday Women’s Club)” (2026), oil on canvas, 72 x 90 inches. Courtesy of Lévy Gorvy Dayan
The artist’s recent work depicts herself as all of the women, who each interact in domestic spaces. Toys, books, maps, and the occasional uncanny scenario, such as the green ladder in the wall of “Re-membering XI (To Leave This Steady Unendurable Land),” nod to a period of significant change in Africa. The figures often play with or alter the items in front of them, such as documenting a transatlantic vessel or jostling a teddy bear in an activity that blurs gutting and mending.
Sometimes, Mathenge’s protagonists meet the viewer’s gaze directly, almost confrontationally, while in other settings, she or he relaxes amid an array of items. Through the lens of cultural memory, the artist gathers symbols of resistance and healing. The compositions are sometimes paradoxical in their depictions of toys and nostalgic items with an underlying tension, like “Re-membering XIII (May the Wind Be Always at Your Back)” in which one of the figures readies an arrow in a bow.
“Re-membering signifies not merely the act of recall, but the active gathering and reassembly of what has been fragmented: cultural memory, inherited forms, histories, and ways of seeing,” the artist says in a statement. The exhibition continues through October 24 in New York. See more on Mathenge’s Instagram.
“Re-Membering II (Facing Mt. Kenya)” (2025), oil on canvas, 91.4 x 88.9 inches. Photo by Brian Griffin Art Photography, courtesy of Pippy Houldsworth Gallery
“Re-membering X (I Fall Upon the Earth, I Call Upon the Air)” (2026), oil on canvas, 20 3/4 × 20 3/4 inches. Courtesy of Lévy Gorvy Dayan
“The Ascendants XXIV (Tea O’clock with Neel’s Ringgold II)” (2023), oil on canvas, 84 x 62 inches. Photo by Brian Griffin Art Photography, courtesy of Pippy Houldsworth Gallery
“Re-membering XIII (May the Wind Be Always at Your Back)” (2026), oil on canvas, 71 7/8 x 82 inches. Courtesy of Lévy Gorvy Dayan
“The Ascendants XXIII (Oblivion)” (2023), oil on canvas, 63 x 63 inches. Photo by Brian Griffin Art Photography, courtesy of Pippy Houldsworth Gallery

title: Louvre Among Major Paris Museums to Shutter During Saturday Protests
description:
News
                The Fondation Cartier, galleries including Gagosian and Perrotin, and Art Basel Paris will remain closed al
body:
News
                The Fondation Cartier, galleries including Gagosian and Perrotin, and Art Basel Paris will remain closed all weekend.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Student protesters block an entrance to the Louvre Museum in Paris, decrying police violence and austerity measures, on October 19, 2026. (photo Magali Cohen / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)
    
        
            Several Paris museums including the Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay, the Musée de l'Orangerie, and the Musée National Picasso will be closed on Saturday, October 24 ahead of planned protests calling for educational reform, lower cost of living, and an end to police violence. The announcement, reported by French media, follows Art Basel Paris's publicized decision to end the fair early on Friday night and close for the two remaining public days. Private foundations and commercial galleries also announced their preliminary Saturday closures. The Fondation Cartier website notes that it will be closed on Saturday and Sunday, while Fondation Louis Vuitton states that it will be closed on Saturday. Some of the city’s commercial galleries, many of which are also Art Basel Paris exhibitors, have publicized their Saturday closures on their websites and social media pages, among them Gagosian, Esther Schipper, and Perrotin. Galerie Lelong's Paris location confirmed with Hyperallergic that it will remain open this weekend. French authorities have moved to ban “illegitimate” protests nationwide and will deploy military troops and increased police presence in Paris and other major cities on Saturday. Demonstration requests filed by registered labor unions will be examined in accordance with the law and potentially required to utilize alternative routes. A forthcoming large-scale union-led rally, originally scheduled for this Saturday outside the Grand Palais in protest of Art Basel Paris, has updated its location to Place de la Bastille after the fair's premature closure and an order to refrain from entering the city center. The National Union of Visual Artists (SNAP–CGT), which called for the rally outside Art Basel Paris, told Hyperallergic that the protest’s aim is “to defend culture for everyone and decent conditions for art workers.”“That the fair is canceling its weekend under pressure from the social movement is a victory,” said a representative from the group. “Let us keep the movement going, in support of the demands of high-school and university students and to build the strike.”

title: Meet the Painter Adorning Phoebe Bridgers’s Guitars
description:
Feature
                The musician and indie darling was drawn to John Griswold's intimate tableaux evoking Renaissance and Ba
body:
Feature
                The musician and indie darling was drawn to John Griswold's intimate tableaux evoking Renaissance and Baroque iconographies.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Phoebe Bridgers's guitar custom-painted by John Griswold (photo by and courtesy Wes Ellis)
    
        
            On an average day in December 2022, the Pasadena-based surrealist classicist painter John Griswold got an Instagram DM from musician Phoebe Bridgers. “I remember she said ‘big fan,’” Griswold told Hyperallergic, “and I thought that was pretty funny, given the fact that, to quote a common epithet of hers, she’s ‘Phoebe Fucking Bridgers.’” The indie darling went on to ask Griswold if he had ever painted on a guitar, and from there a collaborative artistic relationship was born. Griswold, known for his intimate tableaux and animated collages that evoke Renaissance and Baroque iconographies, has now painted multiple instruments for Bridgers, including another guitar she has been taking on tour as well as a lyric book, a vinyl cover, and a secret puzzle for her much-anticipated third solo album, Lost Weekend. The world saw Griswold’s most personal commission for Bridgers, a custom-painted vintage Gibson guitar, for the first time when the singer performed on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon earlier this year. The small oil paintings jump off the aged black surface, echoing Bridgers’s ice-blonde hair sparkling against her black wardrobe. Phoebe Bridgers in the artist's studio (photo courtesy John Griswold)The two artists, though fluent in different mediums, spoke the same creative language and worked hand in hand over the course of four years to finalize a vision for the guitar. Neither artist wanted to change the instrument's surface or alter its visible wear. Griswold used oil paints mixed with an alkyd medium to create the images, and the final product is a guitar that is completely personal to Bridgers.

title: Kid Cudi to Write, Direct, and Star as Basquiat in New Biopic
description:
Film
                The rapper called his forthcoming film, "JEAN," a “love letter” to the late artist and ’80s New York in his
body:
Film
                The rapper called his forthcoming film, "JEAN," a “love letter” to the late artist and ’80s New York in his announcement on October 21.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Left: American artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960–88), c. 1985 (photo Rose Hartman via Getty Images); right: Kid Cudi in 2025 (photo Alan Chapman/Dave Benett via Getty Images)
    
        
            American rapper Kid Cudi took to Instagram this week to announce his hand in writing, directing, and starring in the forthcoming project JEAN, a biopic of late contemporary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat. Cudi called the film a “love letter to Jean, the 80s and NY city,” and said that production is set to begin next year.Cudi added that he will portray Basquiat, stating that the late artist has served as an inspiration to his career throughout, and that it'll be the “biggest honor to tell his story in a way we haven't seen before.”“This one im so proud of and excited about,” Cudi wrote in the caption accompanying the mockup promotional poster and several black-and-white photos of him as Basquiat in a large studio. “To write a film about someone who existed was a challenge, but it was a welcomed one. A lot of research, books, talks with people that knew him.”The announcement of JEAN comes after Cudi publicized his own foray into visual art in recent months. The multi-hyphenate artist debuted his painting practice under the name Scotty Ramon in a group presentation at Art Cologne 2025, and held his inaugural solo exhibition, Echoes of the Past, at the Paris location of Ruttkowski;68 this January. Scotty Ramon (Kid Cudi) shares one of his paintings, “WHEN THE LIGHT DIES,” on Instagram (screenshot Hyperallergic via Instagram)

title: Skirball Cultural Center presents “The 1960s — A Generation on Fire: Judy Baca’s Great Wall of Los Angeles”
description:
Announcement
                The exhibition shares two new sections of the public art mural on view for the first time, featurin
body:
Announcement
                The exhibition shares two new sections of the public art mural on view for the first time, featuring moments from an era of collective action that still resonates today.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Judy Baca, detail from the 1960s segment of the Great Wall of Los Angeles mural. Courtesy of the artist Judy Baca and the SPARC Archives.
    
        
            One of California’s most culturally significant landmarks comes to the Skirball with the opening of The 1960s — A Generation on Fire: Judy Baca's Great Wall of Los Angeles featuring new, monumental murals that approach history as a living, contested, and shared narrative in which we all take part. In 1974, Judy Baca conceived of the Great Wall as a monument to the people of California, featuring a visual history of ethnic peoples from prehistoric times to the 1950s. Soon after in 1976, Baca co-founded the Social and Public Art Resource Center (SPARC) and together with 400 young people working alongside artists, historians, and community members, collaborated to paint the first section of the half-mile mural on the LA River. Since then, Baca and SPARC have been working to extend the mural beyond the 1950s to present day.Within this exhibition, viewers can observe how the decade was shaped by the moral courage, peaceful protests, and cultural awakening of the Civil Rights Movement and the “generation on fire” who led the way. Visitors will also see recently completed mural sections focused on the 1960s that will soon be added to the existing mural. The murals are presented alongside preparatory drawings and color studies; an immersive video installation that brings visitors to the banks of the LA River at the Tujunga Wash, the ultimate site for the murals; as well as an interactive component called MuralMemoirs where visitors can share their own histories.The 1960s — A Generation on Fire: Judy Baca’s Great Wall of Los Angeles is on view at the Skirball, where individual sections will be revealed throughout the exhibition run from October to December 2026 and January to February 2027. Learn more at skirball.org.
